messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric transducer (Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$).
    *   Output: $V_{out}$ across load $R_L$ and storage capacitor $C_{out}$.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Operating Conditions:
        *   S1: Nominal ($I_p=50\mu\text{A}$, $f=100\text{Hz}$, $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$)
        *   S2: Heavy load ($R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$) -> $V_{out}$ min failure in FBR.
        *   S3: Strong excitation, light load ($I_p=100\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=2200\text{k}\Omega$) -> $V_{max}$ failure in FBR.
        *   S4: Weak excitation ($I_p=30\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=1000\text{k}\Omega$) -> $V_{out}$ min failure in FBR.
        *   S5: Low freq ($f=80\text{Hz}$, $R_L=470\text{k}\Omega$) -> Settled failure in FBR.
        *   S6: Hot, higher $C_p$ ($C_p=30\text{nF}$, $R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$).

    *   The FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) is too simple.
    *   Low output voltage in S2/S4 is due to diode drops (DSCH is $\sim 0.25\text{V}$, total $0.5\text{V}$ drop) and inefficiency.
    *   High output voltage in S3 is because the rectification isn't regulated.
    *   $V_{pp}$ (ripple) can be managed by $C_{out}$ (but too large $C_{out}$ might slow down $t_{up}$).
    *   The open-circuit voltage is low ($\sim 3.2\text{V}$ peak).

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* This is the gold standard for piezo energy harvesting. It uses an inductor and switches to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the extracted energy.
    *   *Active Rectification:* Replacing diodes with MOSFETs (or synchronous switches).
    *   *Voltage Regulation:* A Zener diode or a shunt regulator to prevent $V_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$.

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI (Parallel-SSHI or similar)**
        *   The basic SSHI uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage across $C_p$ when it reaches a peak.
        *   Circuit: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ Storage. SSHI circuitry works in parallel with the piezo to flip the charge.
        *   Simplified SSHI: Use a SYNC switch and an inductor to invert the voltage across the piezo capacitor $C_p$.
        *   Wait, the goal is $V_{out}$. A standard SSHI often uses a bridge. Let's try a modified SSHI: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Bridge $\rightarrow$ Out, with an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ flipping $C_p$.
        *   Actually, a simpler "Synchronous" approach: Use switches instead of diodes to reduce voltage drop. However, we only have 2 SYNC controllers.

    *   **Topology 2: Standard Rectifier with Zener Clamp**
        *   FBR + DZ33 (zener) on `out`. This fixes the $V_{max}$ problem (S3).
        *   But it doesn't fix the $V_{out}$ min problem (S2, S4).

    *   **Topology 3: Synchronous Rectification / Buck-Boost / SSHI-like**
        *   Let's try an SSHI variant. The "Parallel SSHI" (P-SSHI) consists of an inductor and a switch that flips the voltage.
        *   Actually, looking at the components: `S` (switch), `SYNC`, `L`, `C`, `D`.
        *   A common efficient piezo circuit is the *inductor-based flipping* (SSHI).
        *   P-SSHI setup:
            - Piezo connected to a rectifier (DSCH).
            - A switch $S$ and inductor $L$ used to invert $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks.
            - The switch $S$ is closed when $V_{Cp}$ is at its maximum.
        *   Let's refine a specific SSHI circuit:
            - Full bridge rectifier: $D1, D2, D3, D4$.
            - $C_{out}$ on `out`.
            - To implement SSHI, we need to invert $V_{Cp}$. This is usually done by connecting an inductor $L$ across the piezo when the voltage peaks.
            - $S1$ connects $L$ in parallel with the piezo at $t_{peak}$.

    *   **Topology 4: Active Rectification (if possible with SYNC)**
        *   Two SYNCs could act as an active bridge, but we need 4 switches for a full bridge. We only have 4 switches total.
        *   We can use 2 SYNCs and 4 switches to make a synchronous bridge.
        *   SYNC1 controls $S1, S2$ (top pair) and SYNC2 controls $S3, S4$ (bottom pair).
        *   But the SYNC controller is "ideal synchronous controller", which closes switches for `ton` seconds at "piezo voltage extrema". This is perfectly suited for SSHI.

    *   Let's go for:
        1.  **FBR + Zener + Larger $C_{out}$** (Baseline with $V_{max}$ protection).
        2.  **SSHI-inspired circuit** (Inductor-based inversion to increase $V_{avg}$).
        3.  **Synchronous Half-Bridge / Charge Pump** (to boost low voltage).

    *   *Wait, let's rethink SSHI:*
        A classic SSHI uses the inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$.
        Components:
        - $D1, D2, D3, D4$ (full bridge) $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        - $L1$ and $S1$ in parallel with the piezo (pzp, pzn).
        - SYNC1: `edges="both"`, `ton` calculated for $L C_p$ resonance.
        This increases the voltage seen by the rectifier.

    *   *Addressing the Requirements:*
        - $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$: SSHI increases efficiency.
        - $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$: Need a Zener $DZ33$ on `out`.
        - $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$: $C_{out}$ needs to be large enough.
        - $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$: $C_{out}$ cannot be *too* large.

    *   *Designing Proposal 1 (SSHI + FBR + Zener):*
        - $D1: [pzp, out]$, $D2: [pzn, out]$, $D3: [0, pzp]$, $D4: [0, pzn]$ (Wrong bridge! The bridge should be: $D1: [pzp, out]$, $D2: [pzn, out]$, $D3: [0, pzp]$, $D4: [0, pzn]$ - no, that's not right).
        - Correct Full Bridge:
            - Path 1: $pzp \rightarrow D1 \rightarrow out$
            - Path 2: $pzn \rightarrow D2 \rightarrow out$
            - Path 3: $0 \rightarrow D3 \rightarrow pzp$
            - Path 4: $0 \rightarrow D4 \rightarrow pzn$
            Wait, let's check orientation: "forward current flows from the first node to the second".
            - $D1: [pzp, out]$
            - $D2: [pzn, out]$
            - $D3: [0, pzp]$
            - $D4: [0, pzn]$
            Is this right?
            When $pzp > 0$ and $pzp > vout$, $D1$ conducts. $D4$ is reverse biased. $D3$ is reverse biased. $D2$ is reverse biased.
            When $pzp < 0$ and $pzn > vout$, $D2$ conducts. $D3$ is reverse biased. $D4$ is reverse biased. $D1$ is reverse biased.
            Wait, if $pzp$ is positive, $pzn$ is negative.
            - Positive half: $pzp \rightarrow D1 \rightarrow out$ AND $0 \rightarrow D4 \rightarrow pzn$.
            - Negative half: $pzn \rightarrow D2 \rightarrow out$ AND $0 \rightarrow D3 \rightarrow pzp$.
            So:
            $D1: [pzp, out]$, $D4: [0, pzn]$
            $D2: [pzn, out]$, $D3: [0, pzp]$
            Yes, that's a full bridge.

        - Add SSHI:
            $L1$ and $S1$ in parallel with the piezo?
            $L1: [pzp, n1]$, $S1: [n1, pzn]$.
            SYNC1: `edges="both"`, `ton` $\sim \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
            Wait, the SYNC controller triggers at piezo voltage extrema. This is exactly what SSHI needs.

        - Add Zener:
            $DZ1: [0, out]$.

    *   *Designing Proposal 2 (P-SSHI with simpler rectifier):*
        Maybe a half-wave rectifier if the voltage is high enough? No, full-wave is better.
        What if we use a SYNC switch as part of the rectifier?
        We have 4 switches. We could make a synchronous bridge.
        $S1: [pzp, out]$, $S2: [pzn, out]$, $S3: [0, pzp]$, $S4: [0, pzn]$.
        But we only have 2 SYNCs.
        SYNC1: `edges="pos"`, `ton=0.001` $\rightarrow$ controls $S1$ and $S4$.
        SYNC2: `edges="neg"`, `ton=0.001` $\rightarrow$ controls $S2$ and $S3$.
        This removes diode drops ($\sim 0.5\text{V}$), helping $V_{out}$ min (S2, S4).

    *   *Designing Proposal 3 (Synchronous Rectifier + Zener):*
        Combined: Synchronous bridge + Zener.
        $S1: [pzp, out]$, $S2: [pzn, out]$, $S3: [0, pzp]$, $S4: [0, pzn]$.
        SYNC1 (`edges="pos"`), SYNC2 (`edges="neg"`).
        Wait, the switches are closed for `ton` seconds. A rectifier needs to be closed for the *whole* half-cycle ($\sim 0.005\text{s}$). But `ton` is limited to $0.001\text{s}$.
        So synchronous rectification using these `S` and `SYNC` components as described (short pulses) won't work as a standard rectifier. They are designed for *switching* (like SSHI), not for *rectifying*.

    *   *Back to SSHI:*
        The SSHI circuit uses the inductor to flip the voltage. This inversion happens very quickly.
        The rectifier (diodes) is always there.
        Let's refine Proposal 1:
        - $D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]$ (FBR)
        - $L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, pzn]$, SYNC1: `edges="both"`, `ton=...`
        - $DZ1: [0, out]$ (Zener)
        - $C1: [out, 0]$ (Storage)

        Wait, $S1$ is the only switch. Let's check the SSHI mechanism again.
        In Parallel-SSHI, you have a capacitor $C_{ssh}$ and a switch.
        In the most basic inductor-based SSHI:
        An inductor is connected across the piezo for a short time at the voltage peak to flip the voltage.
        $L$ connected between $pzp$ and $pzn$ via switch $S$.
        When $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, flipping $V_{Cp}$.
        Then $S$ opens.
        Then the rectifier extracts the energy.
        This is exactly what $L1, S1,$ SYNC1 does.

    *   *Checking the constraints:*
        - Components: 4 Diodes, 1 Zener, 1 Inductor, 1 Switch, 1 SYNC, 1 Capacitor = 9 components. (Limit 16).
        - Nodes: $pzp, pzn, out, 0, n1$.

    *   *Let's double-check the FBR again:*
        - $D1: [pzp, out]$
        - $D2: [pzn, out]$
        - $D3: [0, pzp]$
        - $D4: [0, pzn]$
        If $V_{pzp} = 3\text{V}, V_{pzn} = -3\text{V}, V_{out} = 2\text{V}$:
        - $D1$: anode=3, cathode=2 $\rightarrow$ conducts.
        - $D4$: anode=0, cathode=-3 $\rightarrow$ reverse biased. (Wait, $0 > -3$ so anode is at 0, cathode is at -3? No, diode is $[0, pzn]$, anode is 0, cathode is $pzn$. $0$ is higher than $-3$, so it's forward biased!)
        Wait:
        - Positive cycle: $pzp=3, pzn=-3$.
            $D1 [pzp, out]$: $3 \rightarrow 2$ (OK)
            $D2 [pzn, out]$: $-3 \rightarrow 2$ (No)
            $D3 [0, pzp]$: $0 \rightarrow 3$ (No)
            $D4 [0, pzn]$: $0 \rightarrow -3$ (OK)
            Current: $pzp \rightarrow D1 \rightarrow out \rightarrow load \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow D4 \rightarrow pzn$. Correct.
        - Negative cycle: $pzp=-3, pzn=3$.
            $D1 [pzp, out]$: $-3 \rightarrow 2$ (No)
            $D2 [pzn, out]$: $3 \rightarrow 2$ (OK)
            $D3 [0, pzp]$: $0 \rightarrow -3$ (OK)
            $D4 [0, pzn]$: $0 \rightarrow 3$ (No)
            Current: $pzn \rightarrow D2 \rightarrow out \rightarrow load \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow D3 \rightarrow pzp$. Correct.

    *   *Is there a better way to handle $V_{out}$ min (S2, S4)?*
        The SSHI significantly increases the voltage across the rectifier.
        Instead of $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$, SSHI can effectively double or triple the voltage seen by the rectifier, making the $0.5\text{V}$ drop negligible.

    *   *Is there a better way to handle $V_{max}$ (S3)?*
        A Zener $DZ33$ is the simplest way. $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ is a tight constraint, and $DZ33$ breaks down at $3.3\text{V}$. This should keep $V_{out}$ around $3.3\text{V}-3.4\text{V}$.

    *   *What about $V_{pp}$?*
        $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ is very small. This requires a large $C_{out}$ or a very high frequency of charging.
        With $f=100\text{Hz}$, $T=10\text{ms}$.
        $\Delta V = \frac{I_{load} \cdot T}{C_{out}}$.
        $I_{load} = \frac{1.8\text{V}}{150\text{k}\Omega} \approx 12\mu\text{A}$.
        $\Delta V = \frac{12\mu\text{A} \cdot 0.01\text{s}}{C_{out}} = \frac{120\text{nA}}{C_{out}}$.
        For $\Delta V = 0.05\text{V}$, $C_{out} = \frac{120\text{nA}}{0.05\text{V}} = 2.4\mu\text{F}$.
        So $C_{out}$ in the $2\mu\text{F}-10\mu\text{F}$ range should work.

    *   *Wait, one more thing:*
        The `ton` for SSHI is $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        $C_p = 25\text{nF}$. If $L = 10\text{mH}$:
        $ton = 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} = 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{250 \cdot 10^{-12}} = 3.14 \cdot 15.8\mu\text{s} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
        This is within the $1\mu\text{s}-1\text{ms}$ limit for `ton`.

    *   *Alternative approach:* What if we use a charge pump?
        With only 2 SYNCs and 4 switches, we can't build a complex charge pump. SSHI is the most powerful option.

    *   *Let's consider if we need a different topology for S2/S4.*
        The main problem is $V_{out}$ reaching $1.8\text{V}$ quickly ($t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$) and staying there.
        SSHI increases the energy harvested per cycle, which helps both $t_{up}$ and $V_{avg}$.

    *   *Final check of Proposal 1:*
        - Full Bridge (D1-D4) $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        - Zener (DZ33) on $out$ to $0$.
        - Inductor $L1$ and Switch $S1$ in parallel with Piezo.
        - SYNC1 triggers $S1$ at both extrema.

    *   *Wait, let me try one more variant in Proposal 2:*
        Instead of a full bridge, could we use a synchronous rectifier?
        Wait, the SYNC controller only closes the switch for `ton` (max $1\text{ms}$).
        $100\text{Hz} \rightarrow$ period $10\text{ms} \rightarrow$ half-period $5\text{ms}$.
        A rectifier needs to be on for $5\text{ms}$. $1\text{ms}$ is not enough.
        So we *must* use diodes for the rectification.

    *   *What about a different SSHI variant?*
        A "Symmetric SSHI" uses two inductors or more complex switching. But a single $L$ and $S$ is the most basic and should be effective.

    *   *Let's refine the components for Proposal 1:*
        - $D1: [pzp, out]$, $D2: [pzn, out]$, $D3: [0, pzp]$, $D4: [0, pzn]$.
        - $C1: [out, 0]$, value $4.7\mu\text{F}$ (to be safe on ripple).
        - $DZ1: [0, out]$, model $DZ33$.
        - $L1: [pzp, n1]$, $S1: [n1, pzn]$, SYNC1: `edges="both"`, `ton=50\mu\text{s}`.

    *   *Proposal 2:* Just a FBR + Zener + $C_{out}$ (the "Reference Design" but with a Zener). This will fix S3 (vmax) but maybe not S2/S4. This is a good control.
    *   *Proposal 3:* A different $L-C$ configuration?
        Maybe the inductor is in series? No, SSHI is typically parallel.
        What if we use the inductor for a boost converter?
        A boost converter needs a switch and a diode.
        S1: [pzp, 0], D1: [pzp, out]... no, that's not right.

    *   *Let's stick to Proposal 1 (SSHI), Proposal 2 (FBR + Zener), and Proposal 3 (FBR + larger $C_{out}$).*
        Wait, Proposal 2 and 3 are too similar.
        Let's try a "Half-Bridge" SSHI for Proposal 3?
        Or maybe an SSHI with different timing?
        Actually, let's try a "Voltage Doubler" (Greinacher circuit) for Proposal 3.
        A voltage doubler uses two capacitors and two diodes.
        $C_{p}$ is already there.
        $D1: [pzp, n1], C1: [n1, 0], D2: [pzp, out]$.
        But $pzp$ is AC. This only works for one half-cycle.
        For both half-cycles, you'd need a full-wave doubler.

    *   *Wait, let's reconsider the "Symmetric SSHI" or "P-SSHI".*
        A P-SSHI (Parallel SSHI) uses a capacitor $C_{ssh}$ and a switch $S$ to flip the voltage.
        Circuit:
        - Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        - $C_{ssh}$ is connected to $pzp$ through $S$ and a diode.
        This is more complex. Let's stay with the inductor-based flip.

    *   *One final look at the FBR:*
        The reference design failed $V_{out}$ min on S2 and S4.
        S2: $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega, V^2/R_L = 1.8^2/150\text{k} = 21.6\mu\text{W}$.
        S4: $R_L = 1000\text{k}\Omega, V^2/R_L = 1.8^2/1000\text{k} = 3.24\mu\text{W}$.
        The FBR is inefficient because the diode drops are a large fraction of the $3.2\text{V}$ peak.
        SSHI is the best way to overcome this.

    *   *Final check on components limit:*
